title: Multimodal confocal microscopy for surgical guidance of skin resections
text:
Mohs micrographic surgery is a highly effective procedure to selectively remove skin tumors; however, it is
used in only a fraction of skin tumor surgeries because it requires substantial infrastructure and personnel
training. This proposal seeks to develop lower infrastructure methods to assess surgical success during skin
tumor surgery with the long term vision to expand surgical guidance where it is indicated but not currently
being used.

title: Developing oral drugs targeting the insulin receptor using 'Beyond Rule of 5' DEL libraries
text:
More than 8 million Americans still endure multiple daily insulin injections to manage disease, as decades of
research have failed to develop an oral drug—leaving its target receptor undruggable. To address this critical
unmet need, we have created a unique DNA-encoded library (DEL) of >180 billion peptides and small molecules
with vastly expanded compound diversity and complexity for screening—overcoming the limitations of previous
approaches. From our DEL screen, we have identified several novel peptide and small-molecule insulin receptor
agonists that we aim to validate and evaluate to enable development of a groundbreaking oral insulin therapy
that would eliminate the burden of frequent insulin injections and enhance the quality of life for patients globally.

title: The role of RNA editing in organizing the cytoplasm.
text:
The proposed research on the role of RNA editing in organizing the cytoplasm is relevant to public health because
deregulation of RNA editing is linked to neurodegenerative diseases like epilepsy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis,
and schizophrenia. Therefore, the proposed research is relevant to NIH’s mission to develop fundamental
knowledge that will help reduce the burdens of human disability and disease. A mechanistic understanding of
how cells regulate RNA editing will enable the generation of programmable RNA editing therapeutics, providing
novel approaches for treating genetic diseases that arise from Single-Nucleotide-Polymorphisms.

title: Perturbation-response approaches to determining the regulatory networks underlying human complex traits
text:
Genetic variation is now understood to contribute to complex disease through disruption of gene regulatory
networks. However, our limited understanding of the nature of these networks makes it difficult to find mechanistic
links between the genome and disease. In this proposal we will combine perturbation-response data with
sophisticated causal inference algorithms to build large-scale networks integrating gene expression with complex
traits, enabling improved understanding of the mechanisms underlying disease.

title: Cellular and Molecular Mechanisms of Early onset colorectal cancer
text:
Over the last few decades, the incidence of early onset colorectal cancer (CRC) (<50 years old) has been steadily
increased at an alarming rate whereas these rates have been decreasing in late onset CRC (≥50 years old). In
the proposed studies, I will examine the mechanisms of sex-dependent changes during early onset colorectal
cancer progression. In addition, I will explore the therapeutic utility of asparagine synthetase deletion in relevant
pre-clinical models of early onset colorectal cancer.

title: Clinical Laboratory & Biomarker Core
text: The overall goals of the JHUCFAR Laboratory core are to provide JHU HIV researchers, especially those new to HIV, with: a) world‐class laboratory expertise to assist in the optimal design of clinical studies where specialized laboratory assays are essential to measuring study outcomes, b) access to appropriate, validated and, where applicable, certified laboratory assays, c) biomarker specimen repository for the storage, cataloguing and testing of biological specimens, including access to the clinical data associated with those specimens, and d) training to match the needs of investigators ranging from understanding how to collaborate with laboratory investigators, incorporate laboratory tests in a clinical study, judge assay quality and readiness for use to actual performance of the assays in one’s own laboratory. The Core will establish mechanisms to enhance research in HIV prevention, treatment, and pathogenesis carried out by both new and established investigators at JHU through improved awareness of and access to the extensive laboratory resources within the institution and by establishing connections outside Johns Hopkins when needed. To this end, the Core will directly provide expert consultation and assay service focused in 4 major scientific areas—virology, immunology, pharmacology, and metabolomics—as well as providing access to both data and biological specimen repositories to advance science. Beyond these laboratories, the Core will establish best data management practices – from clinic to lab to data analysis – and facilitate connections and collaborations with a far broader array of core laboratories within JHU and in other CFARs nationally.

title: Genetic Counseling (GC)
text: GENETIC COUNSELING SHARED RESOURCE ABSTRACT The Genetic Counseling Shared Resource (GC) facilitates basic science, clinical, and behavioral research necessary to translate genetic discoveries into clinical care. GC has provided clinical genetics services and supported genetic research at Huntsman Cancer Institute (HCI) since 2003 (supported by the Cancer Center Support Grant since 2009) and has been directed by Wendy Kohlmann, MS, CGC, since 2006. GC is quintessential to HCI’s mission and builds on HCI’s long history of gene discovery by leading practice-changing research endeavors to determine the clinical utility of genetic testing, optimal methods for risk communication and delivery of genetic counseling, and strategies to manage risk conveyed by inherited cancer predispositions. GC is integral to a major goal of the Cancer Center, bringing scientific discoveries to the clinic and into applications for the population. GC provides several key services necessary for translational genetic research, including identifying cohorts of patients for gene research or studies of syndromes; helping investigators design studies to optimally incorporate genetic information and to anticipate and address ethical, legal, and social issues related to genetic analysis; providing genetic counseling interventions; and collecting clinical phenotypes and longitudinal outcomes data. The aims of GC are 1) to provide cancer genetics expertise, genetic counseling services, and interventions, and 2) to support the scientific research objectives of the Cancer Center, especially in the context of translation of genetics to the clinic and population. Access to research genetic counseling services has allowed Cancer Center members to study novel approaches for providing genetic information and to include participants across our catchment area, the State of Utah. GC adds value to the Cancer Center by ensuring genetics expertise is available to all Cancer Center members and clinical investigators. The broad impact of GC across HCI is indicated by its contribution to 61 publications since 2014. Cancer Center members with peer-reviewed funding comprise 53% of the users, and 100% of GC’s work is cancer-related. HCI’s establishment of a top-quality, research-oriented Genetic Counseling Shared Resource is highly innovative and unique among National Cancer Institute cancer centers. The Director and staff of the Shared Resource participate in national committees, and they extend the impact of HCI research by incorporating findings into guidelines for genetic testing and management of hereditary cancer. GC allows HCI to excel in all areas of hereditary cancer research and to be a leader in genetic discoveries and translation of findings into clinical implementation and population policy.

title: Artificial Intelligence Enabled Tools for Systems Biology Analyses of Next Generation Phospho-Proteomic Data
text:
The objective of this competitive renewal application is to develop algorithms and software to apply state-of-the-
art artificial intelligence techniques to the analysis of emerging high-coverage and high quality phosphor-
proteomics data, with a view to developing tools for annotating understudied kinases, supervised inference of
active kinase networks, and identification of companion kinases for polypharmacy applications.

title: The SMAD3 signaling network in coronary artery disease risk
text:
(Public Health Relevance)
Significant expense and effort by groups of scientists around the world has identified regions of the human
genome that are associated with the genetic risk for various forms of cardiovascular disease, including
coronary artery disease. Additional research is required to understand the specific genes involved, and how
they work to contribute to the disease process. Such information will allow for better risk assessment and the
development of better therapeutics for these diseases.

title: Parent-Child Interaction and Emotion Regulation in Preschoolers with Autism Spectrum Disorder
text:
Emotion regulation (ER) impairments in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exacerbate social
difficulties and contribute to high rates of co-occurring psychiatric and behavioral problems, psychotropic
medication prescription, and inpatient hospitalizations in this population. The proposed study will be a first step
toward identifying early mechanisms and markers of ER impairment by examining emotional dynamics in
parent-child interactions and their relation to ER development. By examining time-linked biological and
behavioral markers of child emotional distress and parent responses, and applying machine learning
approaches to examine multimodal relations between variables, the study has the potential to identify specific
targets for interventions focused on ER development within the parent-child dyad.

title: Automated Live-Cell Imaging Platform with Convertible Fluorescence Microscope
text:
The Discover Echo Revolution microscope will advance research at NSU by enabling high-resolution imaging
of cells (live and fixed), organoids, and tissue sections to support multiple NIH-funded research projects. It will
also enhance student training and coursework in cancer, neuroscience, immunology, and dental research,
while supporting external users and collaborators through our Imaging Core Facility. This shared instrument
will strengthen biomedical research and education across NSU's Colleges of Psychology, Pharmacy, Dental,
and Allopathic Medicine, as well as supporting our community research partners.

title: Targeting oncogenic KRAS to sensitize pancreatic cancer to NK cell immunotherapy
text:
Mutations in the KRAS oncogene are found in >90% of pancreatic cancers, an aggressive malignancy with a
5-year survival of 13% that remains resistant to existing immunotherapies. This study investigates the signaling
mechanisms by which KRAS oncoprotein inhibition regulates NK cell responses in pancreatic cancer and
seeks to establish pre-clinical evidence for a novel, KRAS inhibitor and B7-H3 NK cell engager combination
immunotherapy for patients.

title: Ex vivo intraoperative surgical basal margin analysis in head and neck cancer resection: clinical validation
text:
Relevance to public health
The project will advance and clinically test an automated intraoperative fluorescence imaging technology to help
cancer surgeons remove 100% of primary tumors when possible, reducing the need for follow up treatments like
call-back surgery, radiation therapy, and/or chemoradiotherapy. Moreover, successful primary surgery can
decrease patient morbidity and yield higher survival rates. The proposed fluorescence imaging technology will
be evaluated for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma surgery against state-of-the-art surgical guidance
methods in an 80-patient clinical study, as a precursor to a future phase II clinical trial where the technology is
expected to have positive impact on patient survival and quality of life.

title: Biomedical Imaging for Clinician Scientists
text:
There is a critical shortage of Academic Radiologists who are rigorously trained in Biomedical Imaging Research.
These highly skilled and trained individuals are crucial to advance research in imaging and image-guided
therapies, which will directly impact patient care. This new generation of Academic Radiologists will be essential
to maximize the healthcare benefits that will come from interdisciplinary translational research linking advances
in the sciences of genomics, proteomics and artificial intelligence with the ongoing technological evolution in
Biomedical Imaging

title: Glucose patterns and clinical outcomes in the Dallas Heart Study: A pathway to precision diabetes
text:
Diabetes and prediabetes are common, but highly heterogenous conditions, associated with adverse health
consequences. This project will use continuous glucose monitoring and machine learning techniques to
characterize unique glucose patterns in persons with and without diabetes to identify persons at high risk for
developing diabetes and its cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic consequences.

title: Role of GM-CSF and impaired lipid metabolism in the pathogenesis of PAP
text:
Despite recent advances in therapeutic options showing promising results for patients with pulmonary alveolar
proteinosis (PAP), there is still no FDA-approved therapy, and not all patients respond to these therapies. There
is a critical need to understand the pathogenic mechanisms that underlie PAP in order to develop novel therapies.
This proposal is the first step to unveil these mechanisms by evaluating how disruption in granulocyte-
macrophage colony-stimulating factor signaling leads to lipid dysregulation and surfactant accumulation in the
alveolar space.

title: Finite Elements For Biomechanics And Biophysics
text:
This project will greatly expand the simulation capabilities of the FEBio software suite, which enables computer
simulations in the fields of biomechanics and biophysics. This software already supports over 20,000 scientists
in their research. The outcomes of the proposed research will expand scientific discovery and innovation by
biomedical simulation scientists in the areas of biomechanics and biophysics.

title: Next-generation protein neurotherapeutics for botulism poisoning
text:
Botulinum neurotoxins are highly potent microbial toxins that enter motor neurons and cleaving SNARE proteins
essential for neurotransmitter release, resulting in flaccid paralysis and, in severe cases, lethal respiratory failure.
We propose to create Post-Symptomatic Anti-Botulinum Therapeutics (PSABT), which combine broad-spectrum
nanobodies that potently inhibit the catalytic activity of BoNT LC for all subtypes of serotypes A and B, fused to
a non-toxic toxin-based neuronal delivery vehicle that mimics the same trafficking pathway as the native toxin,
and enables the intracellular delivery of immunotherapies for the treatment of BoNT intoxication. The results of
these studies will establish a foundation for advancing PSABTs towards clinical applications and the
development of therapeutics targeting all subtypes within each remaining serotype.

title: Center for Multi-Scale Analysis of the Human Epitranscriptome
text:
Chemical modifications to RNA molecules—including mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA—are emerging as critical
regulators of gene expression, yet remain poorly understood due to a lack of general, scalable tools to map
and quantify them. This Center will develop and integrate cutting-edge biochemical, sequencing, and
computational technologies to decode RNA modifications across tissues, single cells, subcellular
compartments, and spatially resolved contexts. These tools will transform our ability to study RNA regulation in
health and disease, and will be made broadly accessible through outreach, training, and community-distributed
kits.

title: AI-designed mini-proteins as drivers of pancreatic islet production from pluripotent stem cells
text: In this collaborative project, we integrate knowledge from a team of Investigators with complementary expertise to exploit the power of AI-designed mini-proteins that we show can regulate the epigenetic landscape of stem cells and drive a more efficient differentiation of multiple stem cell (SC) lines into functional islet tissue. We anticipate that our interdisciplinary efforts will produce new knowledge and resources to broaden the future therapeutic use of SC-based treatments for diabetes and beyond.
